one_liner: Header-only C++17 wrapper over std::to_chars that returns a stack-based string, replacing allocating, locale-dependent std::to_string.
what_it_does: Provides tostr::to_static_string(value) for integers and floats, returning a cstatic_string<N> whose N is picked at compile time from the type's digits10/max_digits10. Call .get() (or rely on the implicit conversion) to get a std::string_view into the stack buffer. Same call shape as std::to_string but a different, non-owning return type.
how_it_is_fast: It is a thin, noexcept wrapper around std::to_chars: no heap allocation, no locale lookups, no exceptions. All work happens in a fixed-size stack buffer sized per type at compile time. The large win over std::to_string(double) comes from libstdc++'s locale-aware, snprintf-based double formatting being far slower than to_chars' direct digit-generation algorithm; the integer case gains less because libstdc++'s std::to_string(long) is already close to to_chars speed.
when_to_use: Hot-path numeric-to-string conversion (logging, serialization, protocol encoding) where allocation matters
Formatting doubles specifically, where the gap over std::to_string is largest (~13x in this benchmark)
Code that wants a safe wrapper over std::to_chars without manually sizing and managing the output buffer
C++17 codebases that want to_chars-level speed without hand-rolling buffer math
Cases that need locale-independent, non-throwing numeric formatting
when_not_to_use: You need an owning std::string (e.g. stored beyond the current stack frame or in a container) — get() returns a string_view into a local buffer, so you must copy it into a std::string yourself
You need custom formatting like thousands separators or printf-style width/padding — this only exposes what std::to_chars supports
char8_t or other 'extension' integer types — README/tests mark these as untested TODOs
You need release-build safety against conversion failure: errors from std::to_chars are only caught via assert(), which is compiled out under NDEBUG
You need active maintenance or a track record — single author, 1 star, 0 forks, no commits since 2024-01-13

integration.dependencies: none for the library itself; Catch2 and Google Benchmark are only needed to build the tests/benchmarks
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (CMakeLists.txt sets target_compile_features(... cxx_std_17)); a TO_STATIC_STRING_CXX23_CONSTEXPR macro hints at future full-constexpr support once __cpp_lib_constexpr_charconv is available
integration.platforms: any platform with a std::to_chars implementation for the types used; only actually benchmarked on x86-64 Ubuntu 22.04 with clang-18/libstdc++
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the implementation holds no global or static state and each call operates on its own stack-local buffer, so concurrent calls appear independent, but this is not stated or tested by the project
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same single-argument call shape as std::to_string and exposes a string_view via .get()/implicit conversion, but returns cstatic_string<N> (stack-based, tied to the call's scope), not std::string, so call sites needing an owning, heap-backed string must convert explicitly

gotchas: Buffer size N is fixed per type at compile time (rounded to 8/16/32 bytes for integers, or computed from max_digits10 for floats) — it is not user-configurable
std::to_chars errors are only checked via assert(result.ec == std::errc()); in a release (NDEBUG) build a conversion failure is silently ignored rather than surfaced
get() returns a std::string_view referencing the returned object's internal buffer — do not outlive the cstatic_string instance
char8_t and other extension integer types are explicitly untested (marked '// TODO' in test/test.cpp)
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this over Str (MengRao/str) — the only sibling that also targets std::to_string/stoi — when you want a minimal, single-purpose std::to_chars wrapper rather than a broader string/parsing utility library; Str claims larger speedups but bundles more surface area than just numeric formatting.
verified_claims_summary: On an i7-10510U @ 1.80GHz with clang-18, CMake Release, C++20, libstdc++ (Ubuntu 22.04), via Google Benchmark: std::to_string(long) 45.3ns vs to_static_string(long) 27.7ns (~1.6x), and std::to_string(double) 1245ns vs to_static_string(double) 95.6ns (~13x). In both cases to_static_string tracks raw std::to_chars almost exactly (27.7 vs 27.4ns; 95.6 vs 98.4ns), so the measured win is really std::to_chars' win over std::to_string, delivered through a safer wrapper.
status_note: Stale: single-author project, last commit 2024-01-13, 1 star, 0 forks, 0 open issues/PRs (low-traffic rather than actively triaged).
